brief.client: A causeway authority whose crossing times have been a recorded telephone message since 1983
brief.ask: The crossing times have reached people the same way for forty-three years: a recorded line in the keeper's hut, re-recorded twice a day, and a hand-cranked board at the mainland gate. The exchange goes digital on 27 January and the line goes with it. From that morning the times live on a screen, and the screen has to do what the recording did — be read by somebody sitting at the top of the bank with the engine running, deciding whether to go now or turn round. Eleven vehicles were lifted off the sands last year. All eleven drivers had seen a crossing time somewhere.
deliver: The crossing page on a phone, in every state it has: open, closing, closed — and the state it will be in most, cached and hours old.
The gate board at the mainland head, read from a car doing twenty with the sun behind it.
The keeper's screen in the hut: how one person commits a day of windows and shuts the crossing early when the wind turns.
What a stale page does when it cannot know. Drawn, for all three surfaces, not described in a paragraph.
A one-page states-and-transitions sheet the Commissioners can minute and the keeper can argue with.
limits: There is no signal from the top of the bank to the island gate. The page a driver reads is the one their phone cached in the car park.
The board is read at twenty miles an hour through glass the sand has been etching since 2019. Two lines, and the second is optional.
The Commissioners publish times. They do not say it is safe to cross. Any wording a coroner could read as permission has to go.
No countdown that keeps running after the page has lost the tide. A clock that lies is worse than a blank space.

clientProfile.voice: Nobody rings this office to ask when the water comes in. They ring to ask whether they will get back. Answer that, and nothing else.
clientProfile.wrap: The board went in on the Tuesday and the keeper has not telephoned once to complain, which from him is a testimonial. The closed state is now the first thing the island shop looks at in the morning. Invoice the Clerk, not the county.
refs: crossing times on a phone screen

site.tagline: The causeway to Barrowfleet. Open about thirteen hours in twenty-four, never the same thirteen.
site.foot: Where this page and the gate board disagree, the board is correct.

/.p: One mile and three-quarters of road laid on sand. It is covered twice a day and has been since 1847.

/.h: The recorded line closes on 27 January
/.p: The number in the Gate House goes when the exchange goes digital. After that morning the crossing times are published here and on the gate board, and nowhere else.

/.note: These are the Commissioners' published windows. They are not advice, and they assume a car, a dry road and no onshore wind above force five.

/.p: Low water walks forward about fifty minutes a day, so a window that fell mid-morning this week falls at lunchtime the next. There is no pattern a visitor can hold in their head, which is the entire reason there is a board at the gate.

/crossing.h: The rule, as the Commissioners minute it
/crossing.sub: Read out at the Michaelmas meeting and unchanged since 1991.
rows: Two hours either side of low water, less twenty minutes at each end
The road floods at the gate first. Three hundred millimetres will stop a car and four hundred and fifty will move it
An onshore wind above force five brings the water in early. The keeper may shorten a window without notice
The keeper's decision. It is not appealable and it is not explained at the time
Two towers, at 0.6 and 1.3 miles. Nine rungs each. No telephone, no light and no shelter from the wind
Coastguard first, then a contractor. The vehicle remains yours and so does the bill
No policy the Commissioners have ever been shown covers a vehicle driven onto a closed crossing

/crossing.h: If the water is already across the road
/crossing.p: Do not drive at it and do not reverse down the causeway. Leave the vehicle, walk to the nearer tower and go up. Eleven drivers did that last year and eleven were taken off.

items.p: Onshore wind, force six. The keeper cranked the board at 05:50. The recorded line was changed at 06:10, by which time two cars had already gone down.
Both drivers reached the second tower on foot. One vehicle was recovered on the Thursday. One was not.
Salt in the mechanism. The gate was manned on foot for two days and the queue reached the village.

rows: 1961. Case 1984. The glass has not been replaced since
Hand-cranked, two drums of thirty-one numerals
Twice daily by the keeper, on foot, in whatever weather there is
Forty metres, at twenty miles an hour, often into the sun
The drums slip in frost, and a slipped drum reads as a perfectly legitimate time

/gate.h: The board is the last word
/gate.p: Where the board and this page disagree, the board is correct. It stands thirty metres from the water and this page does not.

brief.client: A walking-map publisher that has lettered its sheets the same way since 1968
brief.ask: Every name on our thirty-four sheets is set in a face our own draughtsman cut in 1968 and somebody digitised badly off a bitmap in 1997. The water names are not in it at all — they are adhesive film, and the roll ran out in March. Draw the face properly, roman for the ground and italic for the water, before Sheet 12 goes to the new press in January.
deliver: Roman and italic, upper and lower case, with the accents the Welsh and Gaelic names need
Three optical sizes drawn separately at 4.5, 6 and 9 point — not one face scaled
Tabular figures that column up in a table of spot heights
A proof of the whole set overprinting contour brown and woodland green
A substitution list for the forty-one names that will no longer fit
limits: Water names are set along the water. Every letter has to read rotated to any angle, upside down included.
Nothing thinner than 0.08 mm. Below that it goes into the contour brown and does not come out.
A 1 and a 7 get read in bad light by somebody who is lost. They cannot be mistaken for each other.

clientProfile.voice: People read these names in weather, so I would rather have it right than early.

site.tagline: Walking maps of the northern fells · 1:25,000
site.foot: Sheet corrections posted here, not reprinted.

/.p: Thirty-four sheets covering the ground between Shap and the Tyne gap. Every one walked, and corrected every seven years whether or not anything has moved.

All thirty-four sheets are being relettered for the new press over the next two years. Sheets still carrying the 1968 lettering remain accurate. The names have not changed, only the type they are set in.

rows: 10 m, reduced to 5 m on the limestone
Coated, 115 gsm. It will not tear wet
Four-colour litho until 2026; digital from Sheet 12
Set to the 1968 originals. Water names applied as film
Seven years, on foot, in all weathers

/sheets.sub: Sheets are sold singly. A sheet marked 1968 has not been relettered yet.

/sheets.p: The adhesive italic we have lettered rivers and tarns with since 1971 is discontinued. We hold enough film for two more sheets. After that the water goes unnamed or it goes in a new face.

brief.client: A canal trust replacing the gear on eleven locks, most of whose traffic has never worked one
brief.ask: Every lock on the Nettlebed flight comes out over the winter and goes back with a hydraulic power pack on both ends, which changes the order of operations at all eleven and removes the one thing that used to slow a crew down, namely how heavy the paddle was to wind. Six boats in ten through the flight are hire crews on their second day. Each lock head gets a 178 mm weatherproof panel with no sound, no buttons and no network behind it, and the twelve players are imaged and sealed in the third week of January because nobody is walking back up the towpath to change them, so the sequence has to be cut, tested and frozen before the flight reopens on 27 March.
deliver: The working sequence, eleven steps, 800 × 480, twelve frames a second, looping under forty seconds
A second cut for locks six and seven, the staircase pair, where the chambers empty in the opposite order
An idle state for an empty chamber, ten seconds, that cannot be mistaken for a dead screen
Twelve H.264 files named to the player's scheme, plus a contact sheet of every step as a still for the safety officer to sign
Two sides of motion rules — timing, easing, and what is never permitted to move — so the signage contractor can cut a twelfth lock in 2028 without ringing you
limits: No sound of any kind. The nearest cottage is twelve metres from lock four and the noise consent was won on a promise of silence.
The panel is transflective and refreshes at twelve frames a second at four degrees. Anything smoother than that is a promise the screen cannot keep.
It loops and nobody arrives at the beginning of it. Any four seconds of it has to be the four seconds somebody needed.
Six words on screen at once, set in the flight's signage face, read at three metres, in rain, by someone who has left their glasses on the boat.
The panel has no red in it. Anything that has to read as danger has to read as danger by how it moves.

clientProfile.voice: Nobody at that lock has chosen to look at the screen, and most of them are holding a rope.

site.tagline: Nineteen miles, eleven locks, and the water to work them.

/.p: Nineteen miles of navigation from Thurlby Basin to the junction at Wardlow End, eleven locks of it in the last two and a half. The Trust owns the water, the gates and the towpath, and is answerable for all three still being where you left them.

/.h: The Nettlebed flight is closed from 2 November to 26 March
/.p: All eleven locks come out for hydraulic gear. There is no passage through the flight in that time and no way round it — the nearest alternative is forty-one miles by way of the Ouse. Winter moorings above lock one are free to anyone caught on the wrong side of the closure, and we would rather you took one than tried the Ouse in February.

rows: Marlpit Bridge to the foot of the flight
/.note: Timed at four miles an hour, two crew, no queue. A single-handed boat should add an hour to the flight and start it before noon.

rows: 21.9 m. The short chambers are six and seven
1.06 m, and less than that by late August
2.44 m at Marlpit Bridge, which is the low one
Required. Day licences from the lock cottage, cash or cheque
06:00 to dusk. Last boat into lock one two hours before
/.note: Levels are read at the gauge board at Marlpit Bridge and posted here on a Monday.

/flight.p: A hundred and nine feet of rise in two and a half miles, taken in eleven chambers, two of which are a staircase. It is the reason the navigation was cut and the reason it has twice nearly been abandoned.

rows: Hand-wound until 2 November 2026. Hydraulic power pack thereafter, both ends
About 227,000 litres, all of it down the hill
One, resident at lock four, on the flight from 06:00
Water point, and the only tap on the flight
Half a mile of pound above it. Do not hurry that half mile
Cottage on the offside. Knock if the level looks wrong
Empty the upper chamber first. Always
No pound between six and seven
Pond out of use since 1971 and not coming back
Top gates run heavy in a frost
/flight.note: Rises are to the nearest tenth and move with the level in the summit. Add ten minutes a lock in either direction if you are following a hire boat.

/flight.h: Locks six and seven are a staircase
/flight.p: There is no pound between them. Water leaving the upper chamber goes into the lower one and nowhere else, so the order is fixed, and taking it in the wrong order floods the towpath and empties the pound below. The new gear will not stop you doing it. It only makes it quicker.
/flight.stamp: Read before you work the flight

brief.client: A children's MRI unit that anaesthetises a third of its under-sevens because they cannot lie still
brief.ask: One under-seven in three goes under a general anaesthetic for their scan, not because the imaging needs it but because no child can hold still for forty minutes in a loud narrow tube with nothing to look at. The new suite opens in March with a head coil mirror and a printed ceiling panel rather than a screen, the panels are nine weeks at the printer, so whatever a child is asked to look at for forty minutes has to be drawn and signed off before the end of December.
deliver: Character turnaround: front, three-quarter and back, drawn at ceiling-panel size and again at 40 mm for the wristband
Six panel poses, one per sequence, in the order a routine brain scan runs
The mirror card — the single image that lands in the head coil mirror, proofed reversed
A one-marker version the play team can put on a whiteboard in under ten seconds
Two sides of rules: what the character never does, so our communications office can extend it without calling you back
limits: Everything on that ceiling is seen in a mirror. Anything that depends on left and right is wrong before it is drawn.
One ink on the diffuser, and the room runs at eight lux. Two values, light and dark. A mid-tone is nothing.
No open mouth, no teeth, and it cannot hold the child's gaze. A face that stares back for forty minutes is a face they stop trusting.
Not a species. Half the children on that table will not see themselves in a fox, and two of them on any given week are frightened of dogs.
Nothing on the ceiling moves. It has to be worth looking at again at minute thirty-one.

clientProfile.voice: If a child moves at minute thirty-one we run the sequence again from the start, so whatever you draw has to be worth a second look.
refs: mirror on an MRI head coil

site.tagline: Paediatric imaging. Ninety-one scans a week, most of them awake.

/.p: Two scanners on the second floor, one of them new in March. Most of what happens here is a child being asked to stay completely still for between thirty and fifty minutes.

/.h: Scanner two is out from 16 February
/.p: The room comes apart for eleven days while the new magnet goes in. Urgent paediatric MRI moves to St Cuthbert's for that fortnight, and we will ring every family on the list ourselves rather than write.

/.note: Times run from the first sequence to the last. Add twenty minutes for the coil, the cannula if there is one, and getting a child onto the table without a fuss.

/scan.p: Nothing in the scanner touches you and nothing in it hurts. Two children in three under seven manage it awake. The ones who do not are given a general anaesthetic, which is a larger thing than the scan.

/scan.sub: The desk will go through this again on the day, but it is quicker if you have read it.
rows: As normal, unless the office has told you otherwise on the telephone
Nothing metal past the red line — hair clips, the wire in a bra, the badge on a school jumper
Jogging bottoms and a t-shirt with no transfer print on it
One adult, screened at the desk. A second adult waits the other side of the red line
Loud enough that we give out ear defenders and you hear it anyway. It knocks rather than beeps
Between twenty-four and fifty-one minutes. We will tell you which before you get on the table
/scan.note: Bring the appointment letter. If your child has a favourite thing to look at, tell the play specialist rather than bringing it into the room — almost nothing is allowed past the line.

/scan.p: Blinking and swallowing are fine. Turning your head is not, and neither is talking. A spoiled sequence has to be run again from the beginning, which is why we say forty minutes and mean it.
/scan.stamp: Read this with your child before the day

brief.client: A sea fisheries district whose identification sheet is a photocopy of a photocopy
brief.ask: A new byelaw takes effect on 1 January: berried and v-notched hens go back whatever their size, and three minimum sizes rise by five millimetres. The only identification material this district has ever issued is a 1998 sheet that has been photocopied so many times a berried hen is a grey smudge, so the whole list has to be drawn instead — well enough that a crew can tell a healed notch from a torn fin at four in the morning, on a wet deck, with the wheelhouse light off.
deliver: Fourteen painted species plates at final printed size — lobster, crawfish, edible, velvet and spider crab, and the nine finfish on the prohibited list
A v-notch plate: a fresh cut, a four-year healed cut and a torn fan, drawn side by side at the same angle and the same size
Measurement diagrams at 1:1 for the five shellfish, showing where the gauge sits and where crews keep putting it instead
A double-sided wheelhouse card, A4, for lamination: sizes on one side, what goes back on the other
A one-colour line version of every plate, for the byelaw document and the board at the top of the slipway
A 40 mm cut of each plate for the margin of the landing declaration book
limits: Drawn from animals landed here, not from a book. A lobster's colour is gone twenty minutes out of the water, and what you paint will be held up against one that is still alive.
Every plate has to work in one colour as well as in full colour, and it is the same drawing in both. The byelaw is printed black only.
The 1:1 diagrams get used as a gauge when somebody's gauge has gone over the side. A millimetre of licence there is a prosecution that collapses in front of a bench.
Read on deck at night with the wheelhouse dark. Nothing may depend on a colour difference alone.
Do not make them handsome. The moment a plate is better looking than it is accurate it has stopped being evidence.

clientProfile.voice: Nobody has ever told me the old sheet was wrong, only that they could not make out what was on it.

site.tagline: Sea Fisheries District. Skerrwick harbour wall to Cullen Point, and six miles out.

/.p: Ninety-one miles of coast, eleven landing places, two officers and one boat. Four of the landings have no road to them.

/.h: The 2027 byelaw takes effect on 1 January
/.p: Berried hens and v-notched hens go back over the side whatever their size. Three minimum sizes rise by five millimetres. Nothing is being phased in and there is no first year of grace.

rows: Skerrwick harbour wall to Cullen Point, out to six nautical miles
Two, one boat, one van, and whatever the tide allows
Eleven. Four of them are beaches
At the quay, on the deck, and at the back door of the merchant
Ours is the one that counts. It lives on a chain in the van
Nine. The oldest is 1937 and it is still the one most often broken
Carapace, eye socket to rear edge
Carapace, eye socket to rear edge
/sizes.note: Crawfish, velvet crab and spider crab rise five millimetres on 1 January. There is no tolerance and no benefit of the doubt. If it is sitting on the line it goes back.

/sizes.h: What goes back, at any size
/sizes.p: Any hen carrying eggs. Any hen with a notch or a cut in the tail fan, healed or fresh. Any animal that has lost both claws. They go back whole, alive, and by hand — not tipped from a box off the rail.

rows: A steel gauge, checked against the district standard each March
On your deck, in front of you, from your box
Returned alive if it will live. Recorded either way
Returned. It is an offence to land one and it always has been
Measured twice, by you and then by me, and both written down
To the committee in writing, within twenty-eight days

brief.client: An ironfoundry whose pattern store is being emptied before Christmas
brief.ask: The pattern store holds about four thousand timber patterns, of which twenty-four are still in the price list. The insurer will not renew on the building and the whole shed comes down in November, so the range has to be modelled from the patterns while the patterns are still standing — accurate enough for a merchant to order a casting from, and clean enough to put in front of one who has only ever seen the range as a line of text on a fax.
deliver: Twenty-four castings modelled to the finished casting: hopper heads, downpipe and gutter sections, air bricks, gully gratings, boot scrapers
One PBR material set for weathered iron and one for works primer, shared across the whole range
A single camera and light rig, delivered as a scene file, that every item in the catalogue is shot on
Three views of each casting at 2048 px, and a 512 px thumbnail cut from the same render
Web meshes for the six hopper sizes, glTF, for the ordering page
A written note recording which dimensions came off a pattern and which off a measured casting
limits: A pattern is not the casting. Take the contraction off — one in ninety-six — and the draft angle with it, and write down where you did.
One light rig for all twenty-four. If a boot scraper needs its own lighting to look like anything, the model is wrong.
No ground, no wall, no building behind it. A merchant crops these into a price list at forty millimetres wide.
Each web mesh under 3 MB. They are opened in a yard, on a phone, on the trade counter's wifi.

clientProfile.voice: Every pattern in that shed has the name of the man who cut it on the underside, and not one of them is worth insuring, apparently.

/.p: Nine tonnes of iron a week, most of it in shapes nobody here has redrawn since the sixties.

brief.client: An auction mart that has taken every online bid by telephone since 2017
brief.ask: For nine years every online bid has come into the ring through the office on a phone, and the clerk who takes them finishes after the September sale. From October the screen has to do her job on its own, in front of buyers standing in somebody else's field looking at a photograph of a tractor they cannot walk round.
deliver: The bidder screen through the states a lot passes: open, holding, bid against you, sold, withdrawn
The rostrum view, for the 15-inch screen bolted inside the auctioneer's box
Reconnection — what a bidder sees when the signal returns mid-lot
Registration and deposit, web, desktop and phone
A one-page rule card the office can print and hand across the counter
limits: A lot runs about forty seconds. There is no room for a confirmation step, and a mis-tap is a binding bid of four thousand pounds.
Readable at arm's length, outdoors, in daylight, on one bar of signal.
The auctioneer will look at the rostrum screen twice a lot at most. Everything they need has to be inside those two glances.
No sound. The shed is too loud for it and the field is too quiet.

clientProfile.voice: Nobody here has ever needed a receipt to know what they bought. Do not be the reason that changes.

site.tagline: Livestock on Tuesdays. Machinery the first Saturday of the month.

/.p: Two rings, a canteen that opens at half six, and a car park that is full by seven.

/.h: Telephone bidding ends after the September sale
/.p: The office will stop relaying bids from absent buyers. From October you bid in the shed or on the screen, and the auctioneer takes both the same way.

ps: The auctioneer starts where they judge it will start and comes down until somebody moves. Increments are theirs to set and they change them mid-lot when the ring is slow.
There is no reserve unless the vendor has entered one on the sheet, and if there is one it is not published.

/sales.note: Machinery viewing is the Friday before, 10:00 to 16:00. The yard is not lit after four.

items.p: Cleared in five hours twenty. Forty-one lots went to bidders who were not in the yard.
Two lots withdrawn on the day. The 1998 baler made more than the new one beside it.
First sale where telephone bids passed a hundred. The office ran two handsets.

/online.h: The rules of the online ring
/online.sub: These are the same rules that are read out at the start of every sale.

Binding the moment the auctioneer takes it. There is no undo and no cooling-off period

brief.client: A municipal swimming baths built in 1906, still open
brief.ask: The last of the original tilework spells out DEEP END and NO DIVING in a hand nobody has identified. The council wants new signage throughout and has agreed, reluctantly, that it should match. Draw the alphabet those two phrases imply.
deliver: Uppercase, figures, and the four words already on the wall
Signage cut at three sizes
A note on what you inferred and what you invented
limits: Twenty-two letters are missing. Do not fake certainty.
It has to survive being read through steam.
No revival flourishes the original tiler had no reason to make.
brief.tone: Municipal · warm · older than it looks

clientProfile.voice: Whatever you draw will outlast everyone who approved it.

/.p: Two pools, one of them the original. Open every day since 1906 except for the war and one burst main.
Signage and wayfinding will be replaced during the autumn closure. The tilework on the north wall is listed and is not going anywhere.

brief.client: A hardware shop that has never advertised
brief.ask: Fifty-one years without a single advert, and now the landlord has sold the building and they have one month on the corner they have always been on. One poster. It goes in their own window, facing people who already walk past every day.
deliver: Poster, A1
Window vinyl, one line
A card for the till
limits: It cannot beg.
One colour plus the paper.
Legible from across a two-lane road.

clientProfile.voice: We have never had to say anything before. Now we do.

site.tagline: Ironmongers. Corner of Petty Cury since 1974.

/.p: We sell screws by the single screw. We always have.

ps: Four aisles, one counter, and a man who knows where everything is because he put it there. If we do not have it we will tell you who does, even when that is the shop across the road.

/.p: We are on the corner until the end of the month. After that we do not yet know. Thank you for fifty-one years.

Mixed to a chip you bring in
